subject: Post-demo: hosted fitment + streaming probe schedule
messages:
From: Alex Park <alex@veridian.ai>
To: naomi_feldman@redwood.ai
Cc: eng@veridian.ai
Date: 2027-05-16T15:12:00-07:00
Subject: Post-demo: p95/p99 SLOs and streaming behavior

Hi Naomi — thanks again for the demo earlier. A few follow-ups from our side to help us decide between hosted vs our current provider: 

Quick snapshot of our production shape (today):
- Average TPS (inference requests): ~200 TPS; sustained peaks ~500 TPS for short windows (1–3 min).
- Typical payloads: 1–3 prompt messages, avg 350 tokens in, streaming outputs up to 1,200 tokens.
- Per-client concurrency: 10–20 concurrent open streams (users keep one stream per session).
- Model: Llama2-20B, q4_0, KV cache warm-hit ~30% (we see lots of cold starts on first request).
- Current provider reported e2e p95 = 120ms, p99 = 450ms (their numbers exclude client-side websocket buffering; include network hop in same region).

What we need from Redwood to compare apples-to-apples:
1) Recommended p95/p99 acceptance targets for hosted API (streaming vs non-streaming). Do you present separate SLOs for chunked streaming?
2) Guidance on concurrency limits, recommended connection multiplexing, and how streaming backpressure affects latency measurement.
3) A proposed perf-probe plan we can run against a staging endpoint (we can provide load generators).
4) Any IP ranges or test-token provisioning process.

I attached a small sample of recent traces (veridian_traces.zip) and a CSV with our token distribution. Happy to hop on a short call to walk through. Proposed timeline: we'd like a perf probe by Wed 5/18 to present to our infra committee on 5/20.

Thanks — Alex
Alex Park
Senior Software Engineer, Veridian AI
alex@veridian.ai

(attachment: veridian_traces.zip)

From: naomi_feldman@redwood.ai <naomi_feldman@redwood.ai>
To: Alex Park <alex@veridian.ai>
Cc: ben_carter@redwood.ai
Date: 2027-05-16T17:05:00-07:00
Subject: Re: Post-demo: p95/p99 SLOs and streaming behavior

Alex — great notes, thank you. Recap + proposed next steps below so we have alignment before the probe on 5/18.

High-level fitment takeaways (hosted API):
- We treat streaming and non-streaming as separate observability paths. For streaming we measure two things: first-chunk latency (time to first token) and steady-state chunk latency. For non-streaming we measure end-to-end response latency.
- Suggested starting acceptance window for an apples-to-apples hosted comparison (includes our infra network hops):
  • Non-streaming: p95 <= 140ms, p99 <= 550ms
  • Streaming (first chunk): p95 <= 160ms, p99 <= 700ms
  • Streaming (steady-state chunks of ~200 tokens): p95 <= 40ms, p99 <= 120ms
  These are conservative starter targets we can iterate on after the probe. We’ll also surface token-cost tradeoffs if you want more aggressive latency (different batching / quantization knobs).

Operational asks we need from Veridian before the probe:
1) High-fidelity traffic profile (per-minute TPS distribution for a 1-hour window around peak).
2) Sample payloads and a 5-minute representative session trace (you mentioned the CSV).
3) IP whitelist for our staging endpoint; we’ll issue a scoped test token and an ephemeral endpoint for the probe.

What Redwood will deliver for the probe (attached):
- A perf-probe plan with synthetic workload shapes, test token, and curl/vegeta examples. (see attachment: redwood_probe_plan.xlsx)
- A short-run canary (45–90 minutes) that captures first-chunk and tail metrics, plus raw traces and flamegraphs for slow tails.
- Post-probe recap within 48 hours with p95/p99 graphs, traffic shaping notes, and suggested rollout path (canary -> controlled ramp -> full).

Proposed schedule:
- Tue 5/17 EOD: Veridian provides the traffic CSV + IPs.
- Wed 5/18 09:00–11:00 PT: Redwood runs the probe (we can shard into two 30m windows: streaming-heavy and non-streaming-heavy).
- Thu 5/19: Redwood recap and raw traces shared.

Ben I’m looping you in for streaming-config specifics and the exact test endpoints.

Thanks — Naomi
Naomi Feldman
Account Solutions, Redwood Inference
naomi@redwood.ai

(attachment: redwood_probe_plan.xlsx)

From: ben_carter@redwood.ai <ben_carter@redwood.ai>
To: Alex Park <alex@veridian.ai>, naomi_feldman@redwood.ai
Date: 2027-05-16T18:10:00-07:00
Subject: Re: Post-demo: p95/p99 SLOs and streaming behavior

Alex — quick technical notes / what I’ll configure for the probe. Adding them here so the load generator can mirror our shapes.

Summary of probe config we recommend:
- Streaming connections: keep-alive websocket per client session; we recommend 1 stream per client with server-side multiplexing (we can handle up to 4 concurrent streams per GPU worker depending on model size).
- Chunking: prefer 200-token chunk size for steady-state measurements (matches our kernel batch rewards). First-chunk measurement should be isolated (measure time to first token when KV cache cold vs warm).
- Concurrency shaping: for your peak 500 TPS we’ll run a thinned test: 3 phases (ramp, sustained, burst). For tail probing we’ll inject synthetic cold-start 5% of requests.
- KV cache warm-up: recommend a 20–30 minute warm-up window (we’ll report both cold and warm percentiles).

Example curl/websocket samples (we’ll provide full runbook in streaming-config.json). Short example for non-streaming: 
curl -X POST 'https://staging.redwood.ai/v1/generate' 
 -H 'Authorization: Bearer <TEST_TOKEN>' 
 -d '{"model":"llama2-20b-q4_0","prompt":"<payload>","max_tokens":800}'

We’ll publish precise vegeta/hystrix load files so you can run locally or let us run from our cloud agents (we recommend both for corroboration).

One note on measurement: include client RNG jitter and websocket ack latency in your capture so we can align on what you consider network vs server time.

I’ll attach the streaming-config.json and the vegeta profile to our shared Drive after this note.

— Ben
Senior Performance Engineer, Redwood Inference
ben_carter@redwood.ai

(attachment: streaming-config.json)
